intro_cards.title: What this is about
intro_cards.body:
Rules in a building code are applied by people and, increasingly, by software. Both have to settle details that the text of the code does not spell out. We want to learn how you settle some of them.

Please answer as you would in your own work. **There is no expected right answer.** "Depends" is a valuable answer: choose it whenever the answer depends on something not stated, and tell us on what.

intro_cards.title: How the cards work
intro_cards.body: The clause text is available under the book symbol on every card. Some cards ask a general question. Others describe a case: one situation in which only the stated points differ from a plain, otherwise compliant design. Whatever a case does not mention is as it should be. Cards that belong together are linked and show your earlier answer.

sections.title: Stair handrails (4.7.3.1)
sections.question: Is the handrail in this case in accordance with clause 4.7.3.1(b)?

cards.prompt: Clause 4.7.3.1 states the handrail requirements without mentioning a number of steps. In practice, are they limited to stairs above a certain number of steps?

options.label: Yes, limited to stairs above a certain number of steps
options.detail: Please name the number in the note.

options.label: No, they apply to every stair

follow_up.label: Number of steps and the document or wording it comes from, if you know it (optional)

cards.prompt: A requirement is limited to stairs with more than a stated number of steps. For a flight of stairs, are the steps counted by its risers or by its treads?
cards.hint: A flight that begins and ends at a floor or landing level has one tread fewer than it has risers.

options.label: By its risers
options.detail: The number of risers is compared with the stated number.

options.label: By its treads
options.detail: The number of treads is compared with the stated number.

cards.prompt: A requirement is limited to stairs with more than a stated number of steps. A stair has two flights joined by an intermediate landing. Which count is compared with the stated number?

options.label: The count of the whole stair
options.detail: The steps of both flights are added together.

options.label: The count of each flight, separately
options.detail: Each flight is judged on its own count.

cards.prompt: Suppose handrails are required only for stairs with more than a stated number of steps. Clause 4.7.1.1(b) says that staircases must be designed with stair handrails in accordance with clause 4.7.3. Does a stair with fewer steps than that number need a handrail at all?

options.label: No, such a stair needs no handrail
options.detail: Neither the handrail nor its height is required.

options.label: Yes, it needs a handrail, but its height is not checked
options.detail: Clause 4.7.1.1(b) applies; the height requirement of 4.7.3.1(b) does not.

cards.prompt: Note 1 to clause 4.7.1.1 says that clause 4.7.1.1 does not apply within residential units. Clause 4.7.1.1(b) refers to clause 4.7.3 for stair handrails. For a stair inside a residential unit, for example a stair between the two storeys of one maisonette, is the handrail height of 4.7.3.1(b) checked?

options.label: No, the height is not checked

cards.prompt: Clause 4.7.3.1(b) asks for a handrail "between 800 mm and 1000 mm" above the pitch line. A handrail measured at exactly 800 mm, or at exactly 1000 mm, is:

options.label: Compliant at both limits
options.detail: 800 mm and 1000 mm are inside the range.

options.label: Compliant at neither limit
options.detail: 800 mm and 1000 mm are outside the range.

options.label: Compliant at one limit only
options.detail: Please say which in the note.

cards.title: Two flights, one handrail at 700 mm
cards.assumption: The stair is in the common area of an office building, not within a residential unit. Every other requirement of clause 4.7.3.1 is met.
changes: A stair connects two floors. It has two straight flights of ==4 risers== each, joined by an intermediate landing: 8 risers in total.
The handrail along the first flight has its top ==700 mm== above the pitch line, measured vertically. The handrail along the second flight is at 900 mm.

figure.alt: Side view of two flights of four risers with a landing; handrail at 700 mm on the first flight and 900 mm on the second.
figure.caption: Side view, not to scale — height measured vertically from pitch line to handrail

sections.title: Bollards (4.2.3.6)
sections.question: Does the bollard in this case comply with clause 4.2.3.6(c)?

cards.prompt: Clause 4.2.3.6 applies where bollards are erected at entrances to walkways or pathways. Clause 3.2.2, in the section on passenger alighting and boarding points, says that where bollards are used, clause 4.2.3.6 applies. Does the minimum height of 800 mm in 4.2.3.6(c) apply to a bollard that stands neither at an entrance to a walkway or pathway nor at a passenger alighting or boarding point?

options.label: No, it does not apply
options.detail: The 800 mm minimum is not required by this clause.

cards.prompt: Clause 4.2.3.6 applies where bollards are erected "at entrances to walkways or pathways". A footpath starts at the edge of a paved plaza. Three bollards stand in a row along the plaza edge: P1 on the line where the footpath starts, P2 1.5 m before that line and P3 3.0 m before it. Which of them are "at the entrance" of the footpath?
cards.hint: You can select more than one. All three bollards are 900 mm high.

figure.alt: Plan of a plaza and a footpath. Three bollards P1, P2 and P3 stand in a row along the plaza edge, at 0 m, 1.5 m and 3.0 m from the line where the footpath starts.
figure.caption: Plan, distances from the line where the footpath starts

options.label: P1
options.detail: On the line where the footpath starts.

options.label: None of the three
options.detail: No bollard is at the entrance.

cards.prompt: Clause 4.2.3.6(c) gives a minimum height of 800 mm. A bollard stands on a paved area that slopes along the bollard, so the paving at its base is higher on one side than on the other. From which level is the height measured?

options.label: Paving level at the centre of the bollard's base
options.detail: The level directly below the axis of the bollard.

options.label: Highest paving level at the base
Lowest paving level at the base

cards.title: A 700 mm bollard at the far corner of a plaza
cards.assumption: The two bollards at the start of the footpath are 900 mm high and meet every other requirement of 4.2.3.6.
changes: A paved plaza of 4 m × 4 m has a footpath, 1.5 m wide, leaving from one side.
Two bollards stand at the start of the footpath. A third bollard, ==700 mm== high, stands at the far corner of the plaza, about 4 m from the nearest of the two.

figure.alt: Plan of a plaza and a footpath. Two 900 mm bollards stand at the footpath start; a 700 mm bollard stands at the far plaza corner.
figure.caption: Plan — H = vertical bollard height above paving; 4.00 m / 1.50 m are plan sizes

cards.title: A bollard set into the paving
cards.assumption: The bollard stands at the entrance to a footpath, so clause 4.2.3.6 applies. Every other requirement of clause 4.2.3.6 is met.
changes: The bollard object is ==1000 mm== long. It is set ==300 mm== into the paving, so ==700 mm== stand above the paving.
In the building model the bollard carries the property "Height = 1000 mm".

cards.prompt: Clause 4.7.3.1(b) measures the handrail height "from the pitch line". Which line do you use as the pitch line?

options.label: A line through the nosings of the flight
options.detail: The front edges of the treads.

options.label: The tread surface directly below the handrail
options.detail: The height is taken above the step at that point.

options.label: One line from the lowest to the highest nosing of the stair

cards.prompt: Clause 4.7.3.1(b) measures to "the top of the handrails". Which point of the handrail is that?

options.label: The top of the gripping surface
options.detail: The highest point of the handrail profile.

options.label: The centre line of the handrail profile
options.detail: The middle of the part that is gripped.

options.label: The top of the whole railing
options.detail: Including a guard rail above the handrail, if there is one.

cards.prompt: Along one flight, where is the handrail height checked?

options.label: At every nosing
options.detail: Every point must be within the range.

options.label: At the first and the last nosing
options.detail: The two ends of the flight.

options.label: At one representative point
options.detail: For example in the middle of the flight.

cards.prompt: Does the range of 800 mm to 1000 mm also apply where the handrail runs over a landing or extends beyond the top and bottom steps?

options.label: Yes, over landings and extensions too
options.detail: Measured from the floor of the landing or the level beyond the step.

options.label: Over landings, not over the extensions
options.detail: The extensions follow their own requirement in (d).

options.label: No, only along the flights
options.detail: Landings and extensions are not measured for (b).

cards.prompt: In an automated check, a handrail is measured at 1004 mm or at 796 mm. Up to which deviation from the limits would you still accept it?

options.label: No deviation
options.detail: 800 mm and 1000 mm are hard limits.

options.label: More than 10 mm
options.detail: Please give the value in the note.

cards.prompt: A stair has two flights. The handrail along one flight is within the range, the other is not. How should the check report this?

options.label: One result for the whole stair
One result per handrail
options.detail: Whichever part of the stair it runs along.

cards.prompt: A checking software cannot construct the pitch line. Instead it measures from the tread surface directly below the handrail. Would you accept its results for clause 4.7.3.1(b)?

options.label: Yes
options.detail: The difference does not matter in practice.

options.label: Only with a stated correction or tolerance
options.detail: Please say which in the note.

options.label: No
options.detail: The measurement must follow the clause.

follow_up.label: Which correction or tolerance, or why not (optional)

sections.title: When the model does not say

cards.prompt: A building model states the height of an element as a property (for example 1000 mm), but its geometry shows a different height (for example 700 mm). Which value should a check use?

options.label: The less favourable of the two
Neither: report the contradiction
options.detail: The submitter has to resolve it.

cards.prompt: A value that a check needs is missing from the model (for example the handrail height is neither given as a property nor measurable). What should the result be?

options.label: Cannot be assessed
options.detail: The submitter is asked for the missing information.

options.label: The officer checks it by hand

cards.prompt: Some requirements depend on the building type, which the model should state as a property. The property is missing. What should happen?

options.label: The dependent checks are not run
options.detail: The submitter is asked to add the building type.

options.label: The officer sets the building type
options.detail: From the application, then the checks run.

cards.prompt: How should a building model show that a stair lies within a residential unit?

options.label: A space or zone for the unit that contains the stair
Not from the model
options.detail: The officer reads it from the drawings.

cards.prompt: How should a building model show that a bollard stands at an entrance to a walkway or pathway?

options.label: A modelled walkway or pathway the bollard stands at
Not from the model
options.detail: The officer reads it from the drawings.

cards.prompt: Besides the building model, which sources do you use to settle checks like these?

options.label: Application forms
options.detail: For example building type and use.

cards.hint: You can select more than one.

cards.prompt: A check reports a handrail as not compliant. What must you see to accept the result without opening the model yourself?

options.label: The measured value and the limit
Where it was measured
options.detail: In a view of the model.

options.label: The reference used
options.detail: For example the pitch line and the point on the handrail.

options.label: The clause and how the check read it
options.detail: Including conditions such as a number of steps.

options.label: None of these
options.detail: I always check in the model myself.

cards.hint: You can select more than one.

cards.prompt: A check cannot decide because a reading of the clause is open (for example whether the requirement applies to a stair of this size). How should it report this?

options.label: As a separate result "open"
options.detail: Naming the open question and what each answer would give.

cards.prompt: A check uses an assumption that nobody has confirmed (for example a reference line chosen by the software). Should it show the result?

options.label: Yes, marked as resting on an assumption
Only once an officer has confirmed the assumption
No, it should report "cannot be assessed"

cards.prompt: Questions like the ones in this survey have to be settled once for automated checks. Who should settle them in your jurisdiction?

options.label: The authority that issues the code
The team that develops the checking rules
The processing officer, case by case
A joint group of officers and rule developers

closing.title: Finally
closing.free_text_label: Which decisions in applying these two clauses, measuring them in a model or showing the result did we not ask about, but a checker should settle explicitly? Any other remarks?
